narrative:
The model estimates a 57.0% chance that you will leave your job, meaning it considers leaving slightly more likely than staying. Because promotion decisions here treat that retention risk as disqualifying, you are denied a promotion at this time.

The strongest factor in the prediction actually worked in your favor: your overall experience of one to five years was the top-ranked influence and pushed the estimate toward staying. However, that was outweighed by two factors that raised the leave risk. First, you have received other job opportunities while in this job; this was the second most important feature and pushed toward leaving, and it is notable because most employees predicted to stay report no such opportunities. Second, your tenure in this organization of one to five years was the third most important feature and slightly increased the predicted likelihood of leaving. Around half of employees predicted to stay also have this tenure, so it is not unusual by itself, but combined with outside opportunities it signals movement risk.

Next, the organization should discuss your career path and what would make you stay, including concrete promotion criteria, recognition, development, and support. You should also clarify your satisfaction with pay, workload, and recognition, and whether external opportunities are genuinely better. This conversation can test whether the leaving-risk prediction reflects fixable concerns.
